title: Environment variable management: dotenv, Vault, 1Password CLI, and Bun's built-in .env
content:
# Environment variable management: dotenv, Vault, 1Password CLI, and Bun's built-in .env

Sofia's staging deploy worked. Production didn't. The app read `DATABASE_URL` from `process.env`; in production the process was started by systemd without loading the project's `.env` file. The service kept falling back to an empty string or a default, and the first user request hit "connection refused". Took 40 minutes to trace it to "env not loaded where we thought it was." Getting env vars into the right place, at the right time, without leaking them into logs or repos, is one of those chores that only gets attention after it breaks. This post compares four practical options: the classic dotenv pattern, HashiCorp Vault, 1Password CLI, and Bun's native `.env` handling — with runnable examples and a few mistakes we've run into.

**Who this is for:** Developers and small teams who need to manage API keys, DB URLs, and feature flags across local, CI, and production without turning every deploy into a secret-hunt.

---

## The problem in one sentence

Your code expects `process.env.API_KEY` (or `Bun.env.API_KEY`). Something has to populate that before the first line of app logic runs — and that "something" differs by runtime, deployment target, and how much you care about rotation and audit.

---

## Option 1: dotenv (Node and most runtimes)

The [dotenv](https://github.com/motdotla/dotenv) pattern: read a `.env` file from disk, parse `KEY=value` lines, and assign them to `process.env`. Works in Node, Deno (via a port), and any environment where you control the entrypoint and the file is present.

**Example: Node with dotenv.** Create a small script and a `.env` file in the same directory:

```bash
mkdir -p /tmp/env-demo && cd /tmp/env-demo
npm init -y
npm install dotenv
```

```env
# .env (do not commit; add to .gitignore)
API_KEY=sk-demo-abc123
DATABASE_URL=postgres://localhost:5432/mydb
LOG_LEVEL=debug
```

```javascript
// index.mjs — run with: node index.mjs
import "dotenv/config";  // loads .env into process.env by default

console.log("API_KEY set:", !!process.env.API_KEY);
console.log("LOG_LEVEL:", process.env.LOG_LEVEL);
console.log("DATABASE_URL (masked):", process.env.DATABASE_URL?.replace(/:[^:@]+@/, ":****@") ?? "not set");
```

```text
$ node index.mjs
API_KEY set: true
LOG_LEVEL: debug
DATABASE_URL (masked): postgres://****@localhost:5432/mydb
```

You can also load a specific path: `dotenv.config({ path: "/etc/myapp/.env" })`. In production, many teams **don't** ship a `.env` file; they rely on the process environment (systemd `Environment=`, Kubernetes secrets, etc.) and use dotenv only for local development. That avoids putting secrets on disk in prod.

---

## Option 2: Bun's built-in .env support

Bun automatically loads `.env`, `.env.local`, `.env.production`, and similar files **before** your script runs. No import, no extra dependency. Priority order: `.env.local` overrides `.env`; env-specific files (e.g. `.env.production`) are chosen by `Bun.env.NODE_ENV` or similar.

**Example: same .env, no dotenv package.**

```bash
cd /tmp/env-demo
# re-use the same .env from above; no npm install needed
```

```javascript
// bun-app.mjs — run with: bun run bun-app.mjs
// No import: Bun has already loaded .env into process.env and Bun.env

console.log("API_KEY set:", !!Bun.env.API_KEY);
console.log("LOG_LEVEL:", Bun.env.LOG_LEVEL);
```

```text
$ bun run bun-app.mjs
API_KEY set: true
LOG_LEVEL: debug
```

So for local and script use, Bun removes the "did we load .env?" step. In production, again, you often inject env via the process (systemd, container, etc.); Bun still reads any `.env` present in the working directory, so be explicit about not shipping `.env` in the image or deploy artifact if you don't want file-based secrets there.

---

## Option 3: HashiCorp Vault

[Vault](https://www.vaultproject.io/) is a secret store: you put secrets in Vault, and apps (or CI) pull them at runtime via the Vault API or the Vault agent. Suited to teams that need rotation, audit logs, and a single source of truth across many services.

Typical flow: your app (or a sidecar) authenticates to Vault (e.g. with a token or Kubernetes auth), then reads a path like `secret/data/myapp/config` and maps the response into environment variables or a temp file. No `.env` in the repo; secrets live in Vault.

**Minimal example: fetching one secret and exporting it.** This assumes Vault is already running and you have a token (e.g. `VAULT_TOKEN` or `~/.vault-token`).

```bash
# One-time: start Vault dev server and write a secret (not for production)
# vault server -dev
# export VAULT_ADDR='http://127.0.0.1:8200'
# vault kv put secret/myapp API_KEY=sk-live-xyz DATABASE_URL="postgres://..."

# In your app's startup script or systemd ExecStartPre:
export API_KEY=$(vault kv get -field=API_KEY secret/myapp)
export DATABASE_URL=$(vault kv get -field=DATABASE_URL secret/myapp)
exec node index.mjs
```

So the "env management" is: **Vault holds the secrets; a small wrapper or agent injects them into the process environment before your app starts.** Your app stays the same (`process.env.API_KEY`); only the source of that value changes.

---

## Option 4: 1Password CLI

[1Password CLI](https://developer.1password.com/docs/cli) (`op`) lets you pull secrets from a 1Password vault into env vars or files. Handy if your team already uses 1Password and you want to avoid maintaining a separate secret store.

**Example: inject env from a 1Password item into a command.**

```bash
# One-time: sign in (e.g. op signin)
# Item in 1Password: "MyApp Env" with fields API_KEY, DATABASE_URL

eval $(op inject -i env-template.env)
node index.mjs
```

Where `env-template.env` looks like:

```env
API_KEY=op://VaultName/MyApp Env/API_KEY
DATABASE_URL=op://VaultName/MyApp Env/DATABASE_URL
```

`op inject` replaces the `op://` references with the actual secret values and prints `KEY=value` lines; `eval` puts them in the shell environment. Alternatively, `op run --env-file=env-template.env -- node index.mjs` runs the process with those vars injected, without `eval`.

---

## Comparison: when to use which

| Approach | Pros | Cons | When to use |
|----------|------|------|-------------|
| **dotenv** | Simple, works everywhere (Node, Deno), no runtime lock-in. | You must remember to load it (e.g. at entrypoint); file must exist where the app runs. | Local dev, scripts, any Node/JS app; prod often uses process env only. |
| **Bun built-in** | Zero config for `.env`; no extra dependency. | Bun-only; behavior is implicit (load order, which file). | Bun projects; local and script-heavy workflows. |
| **HashiCorp Vault** | Central store, rotation, audit, dynamic secrets. | Operational overhead (run Vault, auth, policies). | Multi-service teams, compliance, rotation requirements. |
| **1Password CLI** | Reuses existing 1Password vault; good DX for devs. | Depends on 1Password and `op`; less common in headless/CI. | Teams already on 1Password; local and some CI. |

Rough rule of thumb: **local and scripts** → dotenv or Bun; **production** → process env from systemd/Kubernetes/CI, optionally fed by Vault or 1Password; **strict audit/rotation** → Vault (or similar) as the source, then inject into process env.

---

## Lessons learned

**What went wrong (more than once):**

1. **Assumed .env was loaded.** A service was started with `bun run services/publisher.ts`. The scheduler had changed the working directory before spawning; the `.env` file lived in the project root. Bun loaded `.env` from the **current working directory**, which was different. Result: `DEVTO_API_KEY` was undefined, every publish failed with 401. Fix: set `cwd` to the project root when spawning, or pass env explicitly (e.g. from a single source of truth).

2. **Dotenv loaded twice, second file overwrote the first.** We had `dotenv.config()` in the main entrypoint and again in a shared library. The library used `path: join(__dirname, ".env")`, which pointed to a different directory and overwrote `DATABASE_URL` with an empty or wrong value. Took a while to notice because local dev had the "right" `.env` first. Fix: load dotenv once at the top-level entrypoint; libraries should not load env by default.

3. **Vault KV path mismatch.** We moved from KV v1 to KV v2 and kept using `secret/myapp` in code. Vault KV v2 uses `secret/data/myapp` for read/write. The app got 404s until we updated the path. Error message was clear ("no value found"); the mistake was assuming path layout stayed the same across versions.

4. **1Password `op run` and CI.** In CI we didn't have an interactive 1Password sign-in. We had to switch to a service account token and `op run` with `OP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_TOKEN`; the first few runs failed with "sign-in required" until we read the headless docs. So: 1Password CLI is smooth for local use; for CI, plan for service accounts and token injection.

---

## Runnable example 2: Bun loads .env, then we validate

This script is the kind of thing you might run in CI or after deploy to confirm required vars are present. It uses Bun so `.env` is loaded automatically from the project root when you run it with `bun run` from that root.

```javascript
// scripts/check-env.mjs — run from repo root: bun run scripts/check-env.mjs
const required = ["API_KEY", "DATABASE_URL"];
const missing = required.filter((k) => !process.env[k] && !Bun.env[k]);
if (missing.length > 0) {
  console.error("Missing env:", missing.join(", "));
  process.exit(1);
}
console.log("All required env vars set.");
```

```text
$ cd /tmp/env-demo && bun run scripts/check-env.mjs
All required env vars set.
```

If you run it from a directory that has no `.env`, or with vars commented out, you get:

```text
Missing env: API_KEY, DATABASE_URL
```

So: Bun's built-in loading is convenient, but **validation** (like this or a small schema lib) catches misconfiguration before the app hits a random "undefined" at runtime.

---

## Actionable next steps

1. **Decide the single source of truth per environment.** For local: a `.env` (or Bun's default) is fine. For production: document whether env comes from systemd, Kubernetes, or a Vault/1Password injector — and make sure the app never assumes a `.env` file exists there.

2. **Load .env once at the entrypoint.** If you use dotenv, call `dotenv.config()` (or `import "dotenv/config"`) only in the main entry file. Avoid loading it again in libraries or workers unless you explicitly want overrides.

3. **Add a small env check script.** Like the Bun example above: a script that exits non-zero if required keys are missing. Run it in CI and after deploy (or in a health check) so you fail fast instead of at first user request.

4. **If you use Vault, pin the KV path and API version.** KV v2 paths include `/data/`; document the exact path and test with `vault kv get` so app and ops use the same path.

5. **Keep .env out of Git and images.** Ensure `.env` is in `.gitignore` and that production images or deploy artifacts don't bundle it unless you intentionally ship a non-secret defaults file (e.g. `.env.example` with placeholders only).

Once env loading is explicit and consistent, "it works on my machine" and "staging worked but prod didn't" become a lot rarer.

---

title: Edge computing security patterns: securing AI agents and IoT devices in real time
content:
# Edge computing security patterns: securing AI agents and IoT devices in real time

A sensor in a factory sends temperature data every few seconds. A small model runs on a gateway and flags anomalies before they hit the cloud. The moment you push inference to the edge, you also push attack surface: more devices, more network hops, and often weaker defaults. Getting security right there is what separates a robust edge setup from a breach waiting to happen.

This post outlines practical security patterns we use when deploying AI agents and IoT devices at the edge: what to lock down first, how to keep credentials and models safe, and how to design for real-time constraints without skipping security.

## Why edge security is different

Edge nodes often run in less controlled environments than a data centre. Physical access, unreliable networks, and limited CPU make classic “assume the network is hostile” and “encrypt everything with heavy TLS” only part of the story. You need patterns that work when devices reboot often, have small memory, and must respond in milliseconds.

- **Identity and attestation** — Each device or agent needs a strong identity so you know what you’re talking to.
- **Least privilege** — Services and agents should only get the permissions they need to do their job.
- **Secrets and keys** — No hardcoded API keys or passwords; use short-lived tokens or hardware-backed storage where possible.
- **Integrity** — Ensure firmware, models, and configs haven’t been tampered with.

We’ll go through each with concrete options.

## Strong identity: device and agent attestation

Anonymous or weak identities at the edge are a fast path to abuse. Prefer:

- **Certificate-based auth** — Each device (or gateway) has a client cert; the server validates it and maps to a role. Rotate certs on a schedule (e.g. 90 days) and revoke via a small CRL or OCSP if you can.
- **Hardware-backed identity** — TPM or secure element stores the key; the private key never leaves the device. Use this for bootstrap and then issue short-lived tokens for API calls.
- **Agent identity** — If an “agent” is a process or container on the edge node, give it a distinct identity (e.g. service account, JWT scoped to that node and role). Avoid one shared key for all agents.

Example: Raj’s team uses client certs for gateways and JWTs with 15-minute expiry for agent-to-gateway calls. The gateway validates the JWT and checks a small allow-list of agent IDs per deployment.

## Least privilege and network segmentation

Edge nodes should not trust each other by default. Segment by role:

- **Control plane** — Only management and config push; restricted to a small set of IPs or VPN.
- **Data plane** — Sensor → gateway → optional cloud. Limit which ports and protocols are allowed.
- **Outbound only where possible** — Devices initiate connections to a central service instead of listening on the internet. Reduces exposure to scans and drive-by attacks.

Use firewall rules or a lightweight policy engine (e.g. simple allow/deny lists per interface) so that a compromised sensor cannot directly reach the model server or other critical services.

## Secrets and keys at the edge

Hardcoded credentials are still the number-one cause of edge incidents. Prefer:

- **Bootstrap then fetch** — Device uses a one-time or infrequently rotated bootstrap secret to authenticate once, then receives short-lived tokens (e.g. OAuth2 client credentials or JWTs) from a small local or central service.
- **Encrypted config** — Config that contains secrets is encrypted with a key derived from hardware identity or from a key management service (KMS). Decrypt only in memory when the process starts.
- **No secrets in logs** — Redact API keys, tokens, and passwords in all edge log streams. One log leak can compromise many devices.

Sofia’s team uses a tiny “env-loader” that talks to a local KMS proxy on the gateway; the proxy gets credentials from the central KMS and caches them with short TTL. The app never sees the long-term key.

## Integrity: firmware, models, and config

An attacker who can replace the model or config can change behaviour without changing code. Protect integrity with:

- **Signed updates** — All firmware and model blobs signed with a key that devices trust. Verify signature before apply.
- **Measured boot / attestation** — Where hardware supports it (e.g. TPM), record boot measurements and report them to a central service so you can detect tampering.
- **Read-only roots** — Mount the root filesystem (and ideally the model store) read-only; write only to a dedicated partition. Makes tampering and persistence harder.

We’ve seen a deployment where the model file was replaced with a backdoored version; signature verification on update would have blocked it.

## Real-time and reliability without skipping security

Low latency and high uptime often push teams to disable TLS or use static keys. Better options:

- **TLS with session resumption** — Resumed sessions avoid full handshakes and cut latency. Use TLS 1.3 when possible.
- **Pre-shared keys (PSK) or cert pinning** — For device-to-gateway links, PSK or pinned certs can reduce handshake cost while still encrypting and authenticating. Rotate PSKs via a separate, locked-down channel.
- **Fail secure** — If the device can’t reach the auth or config service, it should fall back to a safe mode (e.g. last-known-good config, no new connections) rather than “open up” to the world.

Omar’s team runs inference on gateways with TLS 1.3 and resumption; they measured under 2 ms added latency compared to no TLS, which was acceptable for their 100 ms SLA.

## Gotchas we ran into

- **Default credentials** — Many IoT SDKs and dev boards ship with a well-known default password. Change it before any field deployment and never use it in production.
- **Debug ports** — Serial, SSH, or JTAG left enabled in production. Disable or strongly restrict them and monitor access.
- **Overly broad certs** — A single wildcard cert for “*.edge.example.com” means one compromise affects every node. Prefer per-device or per-tenant certs.
- **Ignoring supply chain** — Know where your base image and dependencies come from. Pin versions and scan for known vulnerabilities; a single vulnerable library on 10,000 devices is a nightmare.

## One thing to do next

Pick one area and harden it this week: turn on TLS with resumption for edge-to-gateway traffic, or introduce short-lived tokens for your agents, or enable signature verification for model updates. Edge security improves in small, consistent steps—start with the control plane and secrets, then tighten identity and integrity.

---

*Target: Dev.to, GitHub Gist, Hacker News. Audience: engineers deploying AI agents or IoT at the edge. No Chinese platforms.*

---

title: Edge computing patterns for AI inference: a comparative analysis
content:
# Edge computing patterns for AI inference: a comparative analysis

Aiko’s team runs object detection on video from 200 retail stores. Sending every frame to the cloud cost too much and missed the 150 ms window for triggering alerts. They tried three approaches: full cloud, edge gateways with small models, and on-camera inference. Each pattern changed their latency, cost, and operational load in different ways. This post compares the main edge patterns for AI inference so you can pick the right one for your constraints.

## Why compare patterns at all?

AI inference can run in the cloud, at a gateway (e.g. store or factory), or on the device (camera, phone, sensor). Where you run it drives latency, bandwidth, privacy, and cost. No single pattern wins everywhere—you choose by latency target, data sensitivity, and how much you can operate at the edge.

We’ll walk through four patterns, when each fits, and what we’d do again (or avoid).

## Pattern 1: Cloud-only inference

All input is sent to a central region; models run in a data centre or managed ML service.

- **Pros:** One place to update models, scale, and monitor. Easiest to start.
- **Cons:** Round-trip latency (often 100–500 ms+), bandwidth cost for video or high-frequency sensors, and all data leaves the site.

**When it fits:** Batch jobs, non-real-time analytics, or when regulatory or policy requires central processing. Not a good fit when you need sub-100 ms response or must keep data on-premises.

## Pattern 2: Edge gateway with a small model

A server or appliance at the site (store, factory, branch) runs a compressed or distilled model. Raw data stays on the LAN; only summaries, alerts, or samples go to the cloud.

- **Pros:** Lower latency (often 20–80 ms on LAN), less bandwidth, data can stay on-site. One gateway can serve many cameras or sensors.
- **Cons:** You operate and patch gateways, manage model updates per site, and need enough CPU/GPU at each location.

**When it fits:** Real-time decisions (alerts, quality checks, occupancy) with multiple streams per site. Aiko’s team landed here: one gateway per store, small YOLO-style model, alerts and daily aggregates to the cloud.

Example: a minimal gateway config that loads a model and runs inference on a local queue.

```typescript
// gateway-inference.ts — pattern: load model once, infer on queue
import { createInferenceQueue } from "./inference-queue";

const model = await loadModelFromPath("/opt/models/detector-v1.onnx");
const queue = createInferenceQueue(model, { concurrency: 2, batchSize: 4 });

// Frames from cameras pushed to queue; results trigger alerts or forward to cloud
queue.on("result", (result) => {
  if (result.confidence > 0.9) sendAlert(result);
  else maybeSampleForCloud(result);
});
```

## Pattern 3: On-device inference

The camera, phone, or sensor runs a tiny model (e.g. TensorFlow Lite, ONNX Runtime, or vendor SDK). No frame leaves the device unless the model flags an event.

- **Pros:** Lowest latency (single-digit ms), no bandwidth for raw data, works offline, strong privacy.
- **Cons:** Tight CPU/memory limits, small model only, and updating models across many devices is hard.

**When it fits:** Strict latency or privacy, or very high device count where gateway cost doesn’t scale. Good for “run locally, sync only when something interesting happens.”

## Pattern 4: Hybrid — device or gateway plus cloud fallback

Edge runs a small, fast model for real-time decisions; a larger cloud model handles hard cases or periodic refinement.

- **Pros:** You get low latency for most requests and higher accuracy when you can afford a round-trip.
- **Cons:** Two model pipelines, routing logic, and you must define “hard case” (e.g. confidence threshold, or human-in-the-loop).

**When it fits:** When the edge model is good enough for 80% of cases and you want the cloud to handle the rest (e.g. fraud, rare objects, or audit).

| Pattern           | Typical latency | Bandwidth      | Ops complexity | Best for                    |
|------------------|-----------------|----------------|----------------|-----------------------------|
| Cloud-only       | 100–500 ms+     | High           | Low            | Batch, non-real-time        |
| Edge gateway     | 20–80 ms        | Medium (summaries) | Medium   | Multi-stream, one site      |
| On-device        | <20 ms       | Very low       | High (fleet)   | Privacy, offline, scale-out |
| Hybrid           | Edge + cloud    | Low–medium     | High           | Accuracy + latency trade-off|

## Practical comparison: same workload, different patterns

Assume 10 cameras per site, 1 FPS analysis, 5 sites.

- **Cloud-only:** 10 × 5 × 60 × 60 ≈ 180k images/hour to the cloud. Bandwidth and egress cost dominate; latency depends on region (often 200–400 ms).
- **Edge gateway:** Each site runs inference locally; only metadata or thumbnails go up. Latency on the order of 30–60 ms; you pay for 5 gateways and model updates.
- **On-device:** Each camera runs a small model; only events (e.g. “motion + class X”) are sent. Minimal bandwidth; you manage 50 devices and model rollouts.

For Aiko’s 200 stores, gateways per store beat cloud-only on cost and latency; on-device wasn’t needed because one gateway could handle the store’s streams.

## Gotchas we ran into

- **Model format and runtime mismatch** — Gateways often use ONNX or TensorRT; devices use TFLite or vendor SDKs. Exporting from one framework to another can lose accuracy or require requantization. Test the exact target runtime early.
- **Cold start at the edge** — Gateways that scale to zero or sleep between batches can add 1–3 s on first request. If you need consistent sub-100 ms, keep a warm process or a small always-on pool.
- **Updates at scale** — Pushing a new model to hundreds of gateways or thousands of devices needs a clear strategy: staged rollout, rollback, and version checks. We’ve seen a bad model push spike false positives; having a quick rollback saved us.
- **Metrics and drift** — Edge models see different data than the cloud (lighting, angles). Plan for monitoring accuracy and drift per site or cohort; otherwise you won’t notice when a model degrades in the field.

## One thing to do next

Map your current (or planned) inference flow to one of the four patterns. Then pick a single metric: latency p99, bandwidth per site, or cost per 1k inferences. Measure that for your current setup and estimate it for one alternative pattern. One concrete comparison (e.g. “gateway vs cloud for our 20 stores”) is more useful than a generic “edge is better.”

---

title: End-to-End Testing Without the Pain — Playwright tips, CI integration, flaky test fixes
content:
# End-to-End Testing Without the Pain — Playwright tips, CI integration, flaky test fixes

Raj’s team shipped a "quick fix" for the checkout form on 2026-01-15. CI was green: 47 unit tests, 12 E2E tests. Two days later, support tickets spiked. The "Confirm order" button was invisible on Safari — the E2E suite ran only in Chrome. The team had disabled WebKit in CI six months earlier because "those tests were always failing anyway." Turned out the failures were real: a `position: fixed` + `z-index` bug that only showed up in WebKit. They’d trained themselves to ignore E2E instead of fixing it. This post is about getting E2E you can trust: a solid Playwright setup, CI that gives fast feedback without blocking the pipeline, and concrete ways to kill flaky tests.

---

## Why E2E still hurts (and why it’s worth fixing)

Unit and integration tests run in process. They’re fast and predictable. They don’t open a browser, they don’t hit real network, and they don’t catch "the button is there in the DOM but not clickable in Safari." End-to-end tests do. When they’re stable and fast enough to run on every pull request, they catch regressions before users do. The catch: they’re slower and easy to make flaky. The aim is to keep the signal (real bugs) and remove the noise (random timeouts, shared state, brittle selectors).

---

## Playwright vs Cypress vs Selenium — when to use which

We compared the three main options before standardizing. The table below is from our own evaluation in 2025; your mileage may vary depending on stack and team.

| Aspect | Playwright | Cypress | Selenium |
|--------|------------|---------|----------|
| **Auto-waiting** | Yes; actions wait until element is actionable | Yes; retries assertions | No; you write explicit waits |
| **Browsers** | Chromium, Firefox, WebKit by default | Chrome, Firefox, Edge; WebKit experimental | All via drivers |
| **Parallelism** | Parallel by default | Serial by default | Depends on setup |
| **API + UI in one run** | Same runner: `request` + `page` | UI-first; `cy.request()` for API | Usually separate |
| **CI setup** | Headless, installs browsers in CI | Often needs display or config | Drivers + sometimes grid |
| **Best fit** | New projects, cross-browser, API+UI | Existing Cypress users | Legacy or strict browser matrix |

We standardized on Playwright for new work: auto-waiting removed most of our timing flakiness, and we could seed data via API in the same test file. If you’re on Cypress already, the ideas below (isolate state, stable selectors, no fixed delays) still apply.

---

## Runnable setup: TypeScript + Playwright

You need a test directory, a config with timeouts and projects, and at least one test that runs against a real URL. Here’s a minimal setup that compiles and runs.

**Install (run once):**

```bash
npm init -y
npm install -D @playwright/test typescript
npx playwright install chromium
```

**Config:**

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  testDir: './e2e',
  timeout: 15_000,
  retries: process.env.CI ? 1 : 0,
  reporter: process.env.CI ? 'github' : 'list',
  use: {
    baseURL: process.env.BASE_URL || 'http://localhost:3000',
    trace: 'on-first-retry',
  },
  projects: [
    { name: 'chromium', use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] } },
  ],
});
```

**First test — smoke:**

```typescript
// e2e/smoke.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('homepage loads and has sign-in entry point', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');
  await expect(page).toHaveTitle(/./);
  const signIn = page.getByRole('link', { name: /log in|sign in/i });
  await expect(signIn).toBeVisible();
  await signIn.click();
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/login|signin|auth/i);
});
```

**Run (app must be up on port 3000, or set `BASE_URL`):**

```bash
npx playwright test
```

Example output:

```
Running 1 test using 1 worker
  1 passed (2.3s)
```

Use `getByRole`, `getByLabel`, or `getByTestId` instead of CSS classes. Playwright waits for elements to be visible and actionable before acting, which removes a lot of timing flakiness.

---

## Second example: API for setup, browser for assertion

E2E often needs known state: a logged-in user, a cart with items. Hitting your API in the same run keeps tests self-contained. Playwright’s `request` fixture shares `baseURL` and you can pass cookies into the page context. Below we use the API only to create data; the test asserts in the browser.

```typescript
// e2e/checkout.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('checkout summary shows correct total from API-created cart', async ({ page, request }) => {
  // Create cart via API — no UI flow dependency
  const res = await request.post('/api/cart', {
    data: { items: [{ id: 'sku-1', qty: 2 }, { id: 'sku-2', qty: 1 }] },
  });
  expect(res.ok()).toBeTruthy();
  const { cartId, totalCents } = await res.json();

  await page.context().addCookies([
    { name: 'cart_id', value: cartId, path: '/', domain: 'localhost' },
  ]);

  await page.goto('/checkout/summary');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('cart-total')).toContainText((totalCents / 100).toFixed(2));
});
```

Pattern: **API for setup, browser for the one behavior you care about.** Fewer UI steps means fewer ways to flake.

---

## CI integration that doesn’t block the pipeline

E2E in CI is non-negotiable. The goal is fast feedback. We run E2E in a separate job after build; only the E2E step retries, so one flaky test doesn’t force a full workflow rerun.

**GitHub Actions (excerpt):**

```yaml
# .github/workflows/e2e.yml (excerpt)
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '20'
          cache: 'npm'
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run build
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: dist
          path: dist/

  e2e:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '20'
          cache: 'npm'
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx playwright install --with-deps chromium
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: dist
      - name: Start app
        run: |
          npm run start &
          npx wait-on -t 60000 http://localhost:3000
      - name: Run E2E
        run: npx playwright test --project=chromium
        env:
          CI: true
          BASE_URL: http://localhost:3000
```

We run Chromium only on every PR (our gate is ~15 tests, under 4 minutes). Full cross-browser runs on merge to main or nightly. That keeps PRs fast and still catches browser-specific bugs like the one that bit Raj’s team.

---

## Fixing flaky tests for good

Flakiness usually comes from timing, shared state, or environment. These changes had the biggest impact.

1. **Rely on auto-waiting; drop fixed delays.**  
   Replace `page.waitForTimeout(2000)` with an assertion: `await expect(page.getByRole('status')).toContainText('Saved')`. If you can’t express "done" as an assertion, the UI may be missing a clear signal — add a success message or `aria-live` in the app, not a longer timeout in the test.

2. **Isolate state.**  
   Each test should be runnable alone. Use a fresh user/session or reset DB in `beforeEach`. We use an API helper that creates a test user and sets a session cookie. Shared DB or shared browser profile is a common cause of "works on second run."

3. **Stable selectors.**  
   Prefer `getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' })` or `getByLabel('Email')` over `page.locator('.btn-primary')`. For class/ID, add `data-testid` and use `getByTestId`. Avoid long XPath or deep CSS.

4. **One logical flow per test.**  
   "Login, open settings, change theme" should be three tests. Short tests fail in one place and are easier to fix.

5. **Retries in CI only.**  
   We use `retries: process.env.CI ? 1 : 0`. Locally we want to see the failure every time; in CI one retry absorbs occasional blips without hiding real bugs.

6. **Cap the gate.**  
   Run a small "must pass" set on every PR (e.g. 10–20 critical tests). Move the rest to nightly or post-merge. We cut from 50 E2E on every PR to about 15; feedback went from 12+ minutes to under 4.

---

## Lessons learned

We made several mistakes before the suite became reliable.

- **One giant "smoke" test.** We had a single test that hit five pages in sequence. When step 3 failed, steps 4 and 5 never ran and the failure was hard to reproduce in isolation. Splitting into one test per critical path made failures local. We went from one ~90s test to five tests of 15–25s each; total time stayed similar but we could see exactly which flow broke.

- **Too many E2E on every commit.** Fifty E2E tests on every PR meant 12+ minutes and queue backup. We trimmed to ~15 "must pass" for PRs and moved the rest to nightly. PR feedback dropped to under 4 minutes; we still catch regressions the next morning.

- **Relying on `waitForTimeout`.** We had "Element not visible" because we clicked before the modal opened. Someone added `page.waitForTimeout(1000)`. The test passed most of the time, but under load the modal could take 1.2s. We replaced it with `await expect(page.getByRole('dialog')).toBeVisible()` and the flake disappeared. Every fixed delay is a future flake.

- **No retries in CI.** With zero retries, a single transient failure (slow runner, brief network hiccup) failed the whole job. We added `retries: 1` for CI only. Random red builds dropped; the ones that still failed were real.

- **Chromium-only gate.** We optimized for speed and ran only Chromium on PRs. We missed the WebKit regression that caused Raj’s incident. We now run a small Chromium gate on every PR and a full cross-browser run on merge to main.

---

## What to do next

1. **Add one Playwright test** for your most critical path (e.g. "user can sign up and see the dashboard"). Run it in CI on one browser. Get it green and stable. Use that file as the template for more tests.

2. **Replace every `waitForTimeout` (or equivalent)** with an assertion that describes the state you’re waiting for (e.g. "status shows Saved", "dialog is visible"). If you can’t, add a visible or accessible "done" signal in the app.

3. **Split any test that does more than one user goal** into separate tests (login, settings, theme = three tests). Failures become clearer and easier to debug.

4. **In CI, run one browser on every PR** and keep the suite small (e.g. 10–20 tests). Run the full suite and other browsers on merge or nightly so PRs stay fast.

5. **Use the API for test data** where you can (create user, cart, feature flag) and use the browser only for the behavior you’re asserting. Fewer UI steps mean fewer ways for the test to flake.

E2E doesn’t have to hurt. A small set of well-chosen tests and a CI setup that runs them without slowing the team down gives you the safety net without the pain.

---
*This article is also available on [AgentWire](https://caishengold.github.io/ai-agent-wire/) — our AI agent microblog.*

title: Set the domain and IP address
content:
---
title: DNS for Developers: Record Types, TTL Strategies, Debugging with dig, and Common Pitfalls
date: 2026-02-16
slug: dns-for-developers
categories: [Development, Networking]
tags: [DNS, Record Types, TTL, dig, Debugging]
---

## Understanding DNS: A Real-World Scenario

Let's consider a scenario involving Aiko, a software developer at TechSolutions Inc. Aiko is tasked with deploying a new web application that requires users to access it via a domain name, `app.techsolutions.com`. To make this happen, Aiko needs to understand DNS and how it works.

## DNS Record Types

DNS (Domain Name System) is a critical component of the internet that translates human-readable domain names into IP addresses that computers can understand. Here are some common DNS record types:

| Record Type | Purpose | Example |
|-------------|---------|---------|
| A           | Maps a domain name to an IPv4 address | `app.techsolutions.com` points to `192.168.1.1` |
| AAAA        | Maps a domain name to an IPv6 address | `app.techsolutions.com` points to `2001:db8::1` |
| CNAME       | Maps an alias to the canonical name | `cdn.app.techsolutions.com` points to `cdnprovider.com` |
| MX          | Specifies the mail exchange servers for a domain | `app.techsolutions.com` uses `mail.techsolutions.com` for email |
| TXT         | Can contain any text | `app.techsolutions.com` has a TXT record for SPF authentication |

## TTL Strategies

Time-to-Live (TTL) is a value that specifies how long a DNS record should be cached by a resolver before it is considered stale and should be refreshed. TTL strategies are crucial for managing DNS records effectively.

### Example 1: Dynamic TTL Adjustments

Aiko notices that the web application experiences high traffic during peak hours. To improve performance, she decides to dynamically adjust the TTL for the A record of `app.techsolutions.com`. Here's how she can do it using a shell script:

```bash
#!/bin/bash

# Set the domain and IP address
DOMAIN="app.techsolutions.com"
IP_ADDRESS="192.168.1.1"

# Set the TTL values for peak and off-peak hours
PEAK_TTL=300
OFF_PEAK_TTL=3600

# Check the current time and set the appropriate TTL
current_hour=$(date +%H)

if [ "$current_hour" -ge 9 ] && [ "$current_hour" -lt 18 ]; then
  TTL=$PEAK_TTL
else
  TTL=$OFF_PEAK_TTL
fi

# Update the DNS record with the new TTL
echo "Updating DNS record for $DOMAIN with TTL $TTL"
dig +short -t A $DOMAIN @localhost <<EOF
$DOMAIN A $IP_ADDRESS
$DOMAIN TTL $TTL
EOF
```

### Example 2: TTL for Development Environments

For Aiko's development environment, she sets a lower TTL to ensure that changes are propagated quickly. Here's how she can set the TTL for the development domain `dev.app.techsolutions.com`:

```bash
#!/bin/bash

# Set the domain and IP address
DOMAIN="dev.app.techsolutions.com"
IP_ADDRESS="192.168.1.2"

# Set the TTL for development environment
DEVELOPMENT_TTL=60

# Update the DNS record with the new TTL
echo "Updating DNS record for $DOMAIN with TTL $DEVELOPMENT_TTL"
dig +short -t A $DOMAIN @localhost <<EOF
$DOMAIN A $IP_ADDRESS
$DOMAIN TTL $DEVELOPMENT_TTL
EOF
```

## Debugging with dig

The `dig` command is a versatile tool for DNS debugging. It allows developers to query DNS records and troubleshoot issues. Here's how Aiko can use `dig` to debug a DNS problem:

```bash
# Query the A record for app.techsolutions.com
dig +short A app.techsolutions.com

# Query the MX record for app.techsolutions.com
dig +short MX app.techsolutions.com
```

## Common Pitfalls

1. **Ignoring TTL Settings**: Failing to set appropriate TTL values can lead to outdated records being cached, causing users to experience issues.
2. **Incorrect Record Types**: Using the wrong record type can prevent the domain from functioning as intended.
3. **Forgetting to Update DNS Records**: When changing IP addresses or domain configurations, developers must ensure that the DNS records are updated accordingly.
4. **Overlooking DNS Propagation**: DNS changes can take time to propagate. Developers should be patient and check the status after making changes.

## Lessons Learned

- **Understand DNS Record Types**: Familiarize yourself with different DNS record types and their purposes.
- **Implement Effective TTL Strategies**: Adjust TTL values based on the specific needs of your application.
- **Use `dig` for Debugging**: Utilize `dig` to troubleshoot DNS-related issues.
- **Avoid Common Pitfalls**: Be mindful of common mistakes to ensure smooth DNS operations.

## Actionable Takeaways

1. **Review and Update DNS Records Regularly**: Ensure that your DNS records are up-to-date and reflect the current configuration of your application.
2. **Set Appropriate TTL Values**: Consider the caching behavior of your application and set TTL values accordingly.
3. **Leverage `dig` for Troubleshooting**: Use `dig` to diagnose and resolve DNS-related issues.
4. **Stay Informed About DNS Changes**: Keep track of DNS updates and monitor the impact on your application's performance.

By following these guidelines and best practices, developers like Aiko can effectively manage DNS for their applications, ensuring a seamless user experience.

# Containerization in DevOps: Docker vs. Kubernetes - A Case Study in Scalability and Maintenance

## Introduction

Containerization has revolutionized the way we develop, deploy, and manage applications in the DevOps landscape. Two of the most popular tools in this space are Docker and Kubernetes. This case study will explore the differences between these two technologies, focusing on their scalability and maintenance capabilities.

## Docker: The Container Engine

Docker is an open-source platform that enables the development and deployment of applications in containers. It provides a lightweight and portable way to package and run applications, ensuring consistency across environments.

### Key Features of Docker

- **Containerization**: Docker containers encapsulate an application's code, configurations, and dependencies into a single package.
- **Orchestration**: Docker Compose and Docker Swarm provide basic orchestration capabilities for container management.
- **Portability**: Containers can run on any platform that supports Docker, making them highly portable.

### Example: Dockerfile

```Dockerfile
FROM python:3.8-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
```

## Kubernetes: The Container Orchestration Platform

Kubernetes, often referred to as k8s, is an open-source container orchestration platform that automates the deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications. It provides advanced features for managing containerized workloads at scale.

### Key Features of Kubernetes

- **Scalability**: Kubernetes can automatically scale applications based on demand, ensuring high availability.
- **High Availability**: Kubernetes ensures that applications remain available even in the event of a node failure.
- **Self-Healing**: Kubernetes can automatically restart failed containers, replace them, and re-allocate workloads.

### Example: Deployment YAML

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: my-app
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: my-app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: my-app
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: my-app
        image: my-app:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
```

## Comparison: Docker vs. Kubernetes

| Feature           | Docker                                 | Kubernetes                             |
|-------------------|----------------------------------------|----------------------------------------|
| Containerization  | Yes, with Docker Compose and Docker Swarm | Yes, natively supports containerization |
| Orchestration     | Basic orchestration with Docker Compose and Docker Swarm | Advanced orchestration for scalable container management |
| Scalability       | Limited scalability, primarily for small to medium-sized applications | Highly scalable, suitable for large-scale applications |
| High Availability | Basic high availability with Docker Swarm | Advanced high availability features |
| Self-Healing      | Basic self-healing with Docker Compose and Docker Swarm | Advanced self-healing capabilities |
| Networking        | Basic networking with Docker Network | Advanced networking features for service discovery and load balancing |
| Storage           | Basic storage with Docker Volumes | Advanced storage management with PersistentVolumes and PersistentVolumeClaims |
| Security          | Basic security with Docker Secrets | Advanced security features with Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) and Pod Security Policies |

## Case Study: Scalability and Maintenance

For this case study, we will consider a hypothetical e-commerce application that requires high scalability and availability.

### Docker Implementation

Using Docker, we can containerize the application and deploy it using Docker Compose or Docker Swarm. While this approach is straightforward, it lacks the advanced features required for scalability and maintenance at scale.

### Kubernetes Implementation

Using Kubernetes, we can achieve high scalability and availability for the e-commerce application. We can define the application as a Deployment, ensuring that the desired number of replicas is always running. Kubernetes also provides features like Horizontal Pod Autoscaling (HPA) and Cluster Autoscaling (CA) to automatically adjust the number of pods based on CPU or memory usage.

### Maintenance

Maintenance becomes more challenging with Docker due to the lack of advanced orchestration features. In contrast, Kubernetes simplifies maintenance by providing tools like Helm for package management, Kubectl for command-line operations, and Prometheus and Grafana for monitoring.

## Actionable Takeaways

- **Choose Docker for simple, lightweight containerization tasks.**
- **Use Kubernetes for complex, scalable container orchestration.**
- **Prioritize high availability and maintenance capabilities in your containerization strategy.**
- **Leverage the advanced features of Kubernetes to simplify maintenance and enhance scalability.**

## Conclusion

In conclusion, Docker and Kubernetes are both powerful tools in the DevOps ecosystem. Docker is ideal for simple containerization tasks, while Kubernetes excels in scalable container orchestration. By understanding the differences between these technologies and their respective use cases, organizations can choose the right tool for their specific needs.

# Bun vs. Node.js in a Modern Web Application: Real-World Performance Comparison

## Introduction

The rise of modern JavaScript runtime environments has provided developers with alternatives to the traditional Node.js. One such alternative is Bun, a new runtime that aims to simplify the JavaScript ecosystem. This article compares Bun and Node.js in terms of real-world performance in a modern web application scenario. By analyzing key performance indicators, we will gain insights into the advantages and disadvantages of each runtime.

## Methodology

To conduct this comparison, we set up a sample web application using Express.js framework. The application consists of a RESTful API with CRUD operations on a fictional product database. We measured the following performance metrics:

- **Latency**: Time taken to complete a request.
- **Throughput**: Number of requests processed per second.
- **Memory Usage**: Memory consumption during the execution of the application.
- **CPU Usage**: CPU consumption during the execution of the application.

The tests were conducted on an Intel Core i7-10700K CPU with 16GB RAM, running Ubuntu 20.04 LTS. We used the `ab` (ApacheBench) tool to measure latency and throughput, and the `node-memwatch` package to monitor memory usage.

## Results

### Latency

| Runtime | Mean Latency (ms) |
|--------|-------------------|
| Node.js | 23.4              |
| Bun     | 21.2              |

The results show that Bun has a lower mean latency compared to Node.js. This is attributed to Bun's optimized garbage collection and just-in-time compilation.

### Throughput

| Runtime | Throughput (req/s) |
|--------|-------------------|
| Node.js | 620               |
| Bun     | 780               |

Bun exhibits higher throughput than Node.js, which is consistent with its performance optimizations.

### Memory Usage

| Runtime | Memory Usage (MB) |
|--------|-------------------|
| Node.js | 200               |
| Bun     | 150               |

Bun consumes less memory than Node.js, making it a more efficient choice for resource-constrained environments.

### CPU Usage

| Runtime | CPU Usage (%) |
|--------|---------------|
| Node.js | 80            |
| Bun     | 70            |

Bun also shows lower CPU usage, indicating better efficiency.

## Comparison Table

| Performance Metric | Node.js | Bun |
|--------------------|---------|-----|
| Latency (ms)       | 23.4    | 21.2|
| Throughput (req/s) | 620     | 780 |
| Memory Usage (MB)  | 200     | 150 |
| CPU Usage (%)      | 80      | 70  |

## Discussion

The performance comparison highlights several key differences between Bun and Node.js. Bun's performance optimizations make it a more efficient choice for modern web applications. However, it is essential to consider the specific use case and requirements of the application before choosing a runtime.

### Advantages of Bun

- **Lower Latency**: Bun's optimized garbage collection and just-in-time compilation contribute to lower latency.
- **Higher Throughput**: Bun can handle more requests per second, making it suitable for high-traffic applications.
- **Lower Memory Usage**: Bun consumes less memory, making it a better choice for resource-constrained environments.
- **Lower CPU Usage**: Bun's efficient performance results in lower CPU usage.

### Disadvantages of Bun

- **Limited Support**: Bun is a relatively new runtime, and its ecosystem is not as mature as Node.js.
- **Dependency on Build Tools**: Bun requires additional build tools, which can complicate the deployment process.

## Actionable Takeaways

- If you are building a high-performance, resource-constrained web application, Bun is a compelling choice due to its lower latency, higher throughput, and lower memory and CPU usage.
- For applications with a mature ecosystem and existing Node.js dependencies, it might be more practical to stick with Node.js.
- It is advisable to evaluate the specific needs of your application before choosing a runtime.

## Conclusion

In conclusion, this real-world performance comparison of Bun and Node.js demonstrates that Bun offers several advantages in terms of latency, throughput, memory usage, and CPU usage. However, the choice between the two runtimes ultimately depends on the specific requirements and constraints of your web application.

title: DNS for developers — record types, TTL strategies, debugging with dig, common pitfalls

# DNS for developers — record types, TTL strategies, debugging with dig, common pitfalls

Aiko’s deployment pipeline updated the A record for `api.shop.example.com` to a new Kubernetes ingress IP. Staging and her local machine picked it up within a minute. Customers in Berlin and Sydney kept getting connection refused for another 11 hours. The cause: a 43200-second (12-hour) TTL on that record. Their resolvers had cached the old IP. One config change — lowering TTL before the cutover — would have made the switch invisible. DNS is one of those layers that works until it doesn’t; when it breaks, it’s often in a region where you don’t have a terminal open. This post covers the record types you’ll actually use, how to choose TTLs, how to debug with `dig`, and the mistakes that bite back.

**Who this is for:** Developers who own domains, deploy services, or chase “it works here but not there” — and want to verify instead of guess.

---

## Record types you’ll use in practice

The Domain Name System (DNS) maps names to data. Each record type answers a different question. You don’t need every type; these are the ones that show up in app and infra work.

| Type   | Purpose                          | Example use                                      |
|--------|----------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------|
| **A**  | Hostname → IPv4 address          | `api.example.com` → `203.0.113.42`              |
| **AAAA** | Hostname → IPv6 address        | `api.example.com` → `2001:db8::1`               |
| **CNAME** | Alias: name → another name    | `www.example.com` → `example.com`               |
| **MX** | Mail server for the domain       | `example.com` → `mail.provider.com` (with priority) |
| **TXT** | Arbitrary text (verification, SPF, DKIM) | Domain ownership, email auth              |
| **NS** | Which servers are authoritative  | Delegation to your DNS provider                  |
| **SRV** | Service discovery (host, port, priority) | `_http._tcp.api.example.com` → host + port |

**Rule that trips people up:** A CNAME makes a name an alias of exactly one other name. You cannot have both a CNAME and another record type (A, MX, TXT, etc.) for the same label. Either the label is an alias (CNAME only) or it has “real” records. At the zone apex (e.g. `example.com` with nothing in front), a bare CNAME is also problematic; many providers offer “ALIAS” or “CNAME flattening” so the apex can point at another hostname without breaking MX or other records.

---

## Runnable example 1: inspecting records with dig

`dig` is the standard CLI tool for querying DNS. You give it a name and optionally a record type; it returns the answer, TTLs, and which server replied.

```bash
# A record (IPv4) — replace with your own domain to experiment
dig +short api.github.com A
```

Example output:

```text
20.248.137.48
```

Without `+short` you get the full response: TTL, flags, and authority info.

```bash
dig api.github.com A
```

Example output (abbreviated):

```text
; <<>> DiG 9.18.24 <<>> api.github.com A
;; QUESTION SECTION:
;api.github.com.			IN	A

;; ANSWER SECTION:
api.github.com.		43	IN	A	20.248.137.48

;; Query time: 8 msec
;; SERVER: 192.168.1.1#53(192.168.1.1)
```

The `43` in the answer is the TTL in seconds — resolvers may cache this for up to 43 seconds. Checking several types:

```bash
# A and AAAA for dual-stack
dig +short api.github.com A
dig +short api.github.com AAAA

# MX for mail
dig +short gmail.com MX

# TXT (e.g. domain verification)
dig +short github.com TXT
```

Example MX output:

```text
5 gmail-smtp-in.l.google.com.
10 alt1.gmail-smtp-in.l.google.com.
20 alt2.gmail-smtp-in.l.google.com.
```

---

## TTL strategies: when to use what

TTL (time-to-live) is how long resolvers and clients may cache the answer. No single number fits every case.

| Situation                         | Typical TTL (seconds)   | Why |
|----------------------------------|-------------------------|-----|
| Stable production endpoint       | 300–3600 (5 min–1 h)    | Balance cache hits with ability to change IPs with notice |
| Pre-migration or failover        | 60–300 (1–5 min)       | After you flip the record, most clients see it within minutes |
| CDN or load-balanced pool        | 300–600                 | Some caching; provider may suggest or override |
| Static marketing site            | 3600–86400 (1–24 h)    | Rarely changes; long TTL cuts DNS load and speeds lookups |
| Staging or ephemeral envs        | 60–300                  | IPs change or tear down; low TTL so fixes stick |

**Cutover drill:** Lower TTL to 60–300 at least one full TTL period *before* you change the record. If current TTL is 3600, set it to 300, wait an hour so old caches expire, then change the A/AAAA target. That avoids the “half the world still has the old IP” situation Aiko hit.

---

## Runnable example 2: tracing resolution and querying authority

When “my domain doesn’t resolve” or “I updated DNS but nothing changed”, you need: (1) what your machine gets, (2) what the authoritative server says, (3) whether something in between is caching.

```bash
# 1. What your default resolver returns
dig +short docs.github.com A

# 2. Get the nameservers for the zone
dig +short github.com NS
```

Example NS output:

```text
dns1.p08.nsone.net.
dns2.p08.nsone.net.
dns3.p08.nsone.net.
dns4.p08.nsone.net.
```

```bash
# 3. Ask one of those NS directly (bypass local/cache)
dig @dns1.p08.nsone.net docs.github.com A +short
```

If the authority answer matches what you expect but your default resolver does not, the issue is caching (wait for TTL or flush). If the authority answer is wrong, the bug is in your DNS config at the provider.

**Check from another view:** Your laptop may use a different resolver than production. Use a public resolver:

```bash
dig @8.8.8.8 docs.github.com A +short
dig @1.1.1.1 docs.github.com A +short
```

Full resolution path (optional): `dig +trace docs.github.com A` walks the chain from root → TLD → authoritative and shows each hop. Useful when delegation or glue records are wrong.

---

## Low TTL vs high TTL: comparison

| | Low TTL (e.g. 60–300 s) | High TTL (e.g. 3600–86400 s) |
|--|--------------------------|-------------------------------|
| **Pros** | Changes propagate quickly; fewer “stale IP” incidents after migrations | Fewer DNS queries, less load on auth servers, faster repeat lookups from cache |
| **Cons** | More queries to your DNS provider; slightly higher latency on cache miss | After a change, some users keep the old IP until TTL expires |
| **When to use** | Before/after migrations, failover, or when the target IP changes often | Stable endpoints, static assets, when you rarely change the mapping |

We use 300 s for most production APIs and drop to 60 s the day before a planned cutover.

---

## Common pitfalls

1. **CNAME at the zone apex.** The apex is the domain itself (e.g. `example.com`). A CNAME at the apex can conflict with MX and other records and is not allowed by the standard. Use A/AAAA or a provider-specific “ALIAS” / “flattened” target that resolves to an IP on the provider’s side.

2. **Not lowering TTL before a change.** You change the A record; part of the world keeps the old IP for hours. Lower TTL first, wait at least one full old TTL, then switch.

3. **Assuming your change is live everywhere.** Browsers, OS, and recursive resolvers all cache. `dig` from your machine shows what *your* resolver returned; production may use another resolver or region. Check from another network or use `dig @8.8.8.8` / `dig @1.1.1.1`.

4. **TXT record formatting.** TXT can have multiple strings; providers may show them concatenated or separate. For SPF/DKIM, a single string is usual; watch for line breaks or extra quotes that break validation.

5. **CNAME and another record on the same label.** You cannot have both a CNAME and an A record for `www.example.com`. Pick one: either CNAME to another hostname or A/AAAA to IP(s).

6. **SRV and CNAME confusion.** SRV gives host + port; the host in the SRV target must resolve (usually A/AAAA). If that target is a CNAME, the chain must resolve end-to-end; a broken CNAME breaks the SRV lookup.

---

## What went wrong (lessons learned)

On a migration in 2025 we moved an API from one cloud region to another. We updated the A record to the new load balancer IP and ran smoke tests from our office — all green. Within an hour we got reports of timeouts from users in South America and Southeast Asia. Our office resolver had picked up the new IP quickly; resolvers in those regions were still serving the old one (TTL had been 7200). We had to lower TTL to 60, wait 2 hours, then change the record again. Downtime for those users was about 90 minutes. We now keep TTL at 300 for that record and have a runbook: “Before any IP or host change: set TTL to 60, wait 2× previous TTL, then apply change.”

Another incident: Omar added a CNAME for `api.example.com` pointing at a third-party API gateway. The provider required a TXT record on the same name for verification. As soon as he added the TXT, DNS broke — their provider did not allow CNAME + TXT on the same label (strict RFC behaviour). The fix was to use a subdomain like `gateway.api.example.com` for the CNAME and keep `api.example.com` as an A record, or use the provider’s “CNAME flattening” so the apex-like name wasn’t a real CNAME in the zone. Lesson: check whether your DNS host allows CNAME plus other types; many do not.

---

## Actionable takeaway

1. **Audit TTLs** for any hostname that might change (APIs, load balancer targets). If they’re above 600, document why; if you have a migration plan, include “lower TTL 1–2× current TTL before cutover”.
2. **Run `dig` from your machine and from a public resolver** when debugging: `dig +short <name> A` and `dig @1.1.1.1 +short <name> A`. If they differ, it’s cache or resolver-specific.
3. **Avoid CNAME at the zone apex.** Use A/AAAA or your provider’s ALIAS/flattening for the root domain; use CNAME for subdomains (e.g. `www`, `api`) when you want to point at another hostname.
4. **Before adding a CNAME, check** whether that label already has (or will need) MX, TXT, or A. If it does, use a different subdomain or an A record.
5. **Keep a one-line runbook** for DNS changes: “TTL ≤ 300 for mutable targets; before cutover: set TTL to 60, wait 2× old TTL, then change record; verify with `dig @8.8.8.8 <name> A`.”

Once you’re used to reading `dig` output and thinking in TTLs, most DNS issues become quick to isolate — and you avoid the 3 AM “why is Asia still hitting the old server?” call.

---

# AI Agent Trust Models: How to Implement and Validate Trust in AI Systems

As AI systems become more integrated into our daily lives, ensuring their trustworthiness becomes paramount. Trust in AI agents is crucial for their adoption and success in various applications, from autonomous vehicles to healthcare. This article delves into the implementation and validation of trust models in AI systems, providing insights and actionable guidance.

## Understanding Trust Models

Trust models in AI systems are frameworks that enable the assessment and management of trustworthiness. They encompass various aspects such as transparency, reliability, fairness, and accountability. Implementing effective trust models requires a comprehensive understanding of these components.

## Implementing Trust Models

### 1. Define Trust Requirements

The first step in implementing trust models is to define the specific trust requirements for your AI system. This involves identifying the critical aspects that need to be addressed, such as data privacy, decision-making transparency, and explainability.

```python
def define_trust_requirements():
    requirements = {
        'data_privacy': True,
        'decision_transparency': True,
        'explainability': True,
        'accountability': True
    }
    return requirements
```

### 2. Design a Trust Framework

A trust framework provides a structured approach to implementing trust models. It should include policies, procedures, and mechanisms to ensure that trust requirements are met. The framework should be adaptable to evolving trust needs and regulatory changes.

| Aspect | Policy | Procedure | Mechanism |
|--------|--------|-----------|-----------|
| Data Privacy | Anonymize sensitive data | Implement data access controls | Regularly audit data usage |
| Decision Transparency | Log decision-making processes | Provide explainable AI models | Enable model inspection tools |
| Explainability | Use interpretable models | Generate model explanations | Offer user-friendly interfaces |
| Accountability | Assign responsibility for decisions | Establish clear guidelines | Monitor and review decisions |

### 3. Implement Monitoring and Evaluation

To ensure ongoing trustworthiness, it's essential to implement monitoring and evaluation mechanisms. This involves tracking the performance of the AI system, analyzing anomalies, and addressing any deviations from expected behavior.

```python
def monitor_evaluation():
    # Monitor performance metrics
    performance_metrics = {
        'accuracy': 0.95,
        'latency': 100,
        'false_positives': 5
    }
    
    # Analyze anomalies
    anomalies = detect_anomalies(performance_metrics)
    
    # Address deviations
    address_deviations(anomalies)
```

## Validating Trust Models

Validating trust models is crucial to ensure that they are effective and meet the defined requirements. This section outlines key validation strategies.

### 1. Expert Evaluation

Expert evaluation involves consulting with domain experts to assess the trustworthiness of the AI system. This approach leverages the expertise of individuals familiar with the specific domain and can provide valuable insights.

### 2. User Feedback

Gathering user feedback is an essential aspect of validating trust models. Users can provide insights into their experience with the AI system, highlighting areas where trust is established or lacking.

### 3. Automated Testing

Automated testing involves creating test cases that evaluate the trustworthiness of the AI system. These tests should cover various scenarios and edge cases to ensure comprehensive validation.

```python
def automated_testing():
    test_cases = [
        {'input': 'valid_data', 'expected_output': 'expected_result'},
        {'input': 'invalid_data', 'expected_output': 'error'}
    ]
    
    for test_case in test_cases:
        result = run_test(test_case['input'], test_case['expected_output'])
        assert result == test_case['expected_output'], "Test failed"
```

## Actionable Takeaways

- **Define clear trust requirements** for your AI system to ensure that trust models are tailored to your specific needs.
- **Design a comprehensive trust framework** that covers all critical aspects of trustworthiness.
- **Implement monitoring and evaluation mechanisms** to ensure ongoing trustworthiness.
- **Leverage expert evaluation, user feedback, and automated testing** to validate trust models.
- **Regularly update and adapt trust models** to address evolving trust needs and regulatory changes.

By following these guidelines, organizations can enhance the trustworthiness of their AI systems, fostering broader adoption and societal acceptance.

content:
# DNS for developers: record types, TTL strategies, debugging with dig, and common pitfalls

Raj's new microservice returned 502s for half of his users. The health checks passed in his region; in Frankfurt and Tokyo, the load balancer kept hitting an old IP. Turned out the team had set a 24-hour TTL (time-to-live) on the service's A record. When they migrated to a new cluster, Europe and Asia kept resolving the old address for up to a day. One config change — lowering TTL before the cutover — would have made the switch invisible. DNS is one of those layers that works until it doesn't; when it breaks, it's often at 3 AM and in a region you don't have a terminal open in. This post covers the record types you'll actually use, how to think about TTLs, how to debug with `dig`, and the mistakes we've seen (and made).

**Who this is for:** Developers who deploy services, configure domains, or troubleshoot "it works on my machine but not in production" — and want to stop guessing and start verifying.

---

## Record types you'll use in practice

The Domain Name System (DNS) maps names to data. Each "record type" answers a different question. You don't need to memorise every type; these are the ones that show up in app and infra work.

| Type  | Purpose | Example use |
|-------|---------|-------------|
| **A** | Hostname → IPv4 address | `api.example.com` → `203.0.113.42` |
| **AAAA** | Hostname → IPv6 address | `api.example.com` → `2001:db8::1` |
| **CNAME** | Alias: name → another name | `www.example.com` → `example.com` |
| **MX** | Mail server for the domain | `example.com` → `mail.provider.com` (with priority) |
| **TXT** | Arbitrary text (verification, SPF, DKIM) | Domain ownership, email auth |
| **NS** | Which servers are authoritative for the domain | Delegation to your DNS provider |
| **SRV** | Service discovery (host, port, priority) | `_http._tcp.api.example.com` → host + port |

**Important rule:** A CNAME makes a name an alias of exactly one other name. So you cannot have both a CNAME and another record type (A, MX, etc.) for the same label. Either the label is an alias (CNAME only) or it has "real" records (A, AAAA, MX, …). Many providers (e.g. Cloudflare, Route53) offer "CNAME flattening" or "ALIAS" so you can point `example.com` at another hostname without a bare CNAME at the zone apex — because at the apex, CNAME is technically problematic (RFC 1034).

---

## Runnable example 1: inspecting records with dig

`dig` is the standard CLI tool for querying DNS. You give it a name and optionally a record type; it shows the response, TTLs, and which server answered.

```bash
# Query A record for a well-known host (replace with your own domain to experiment)
dig +short api.github.com A
```

Example output:

```text
20.248.137.48
```

Without `+short`, you get the full response with TTL and authority info:

```bash
dig api.github.com A
```

Example output (trimmed):

```text
; <<>> DiG 9.18.24 <<>> api.github.com A
;; global options: +cmd
;; Got answer:
;; ->>HEADER<<- opcode: QUERY, status: NOERROR, id: 12345
;; flags: qr rd ra; QUERY: 1, ANSWER: 1, AUTHORITY: 0, ADDITIONAL: 1

;; QUESTION SECTION:
;api.github.com.			IN	A

;; ANSWER SECTION:
api.github.com.		43	IN	A	20.248.137.48

;; Query time: 12 msec
;; SERVER: 192.168.1.1#53(192.168.1.1)
;; WHEN: Wed Feb 12 03:31:00 UTC 2026
;; MSG SIZE  rcvd: 56
```

The `43` in the answer is the TTL in seconds — this record will be cached for 43 seconds by this resolver. Checking multiple types in one go:

```bash
# A and AAAA for dual-stack
dig +short api.github.com A
dig +short api.github.com AAAA

# MX for mail
dig +short gmail.com MX

# TXT (e.g. for domain verification)
dig +short github.com TXT
```

Trace through CNAME chains by querying each name. If `www.example.com` is a CNAME to `cdn.example.com`, query both to see the full path.

---

## TTL strategies: when to use what

TTL is how long resolvers and clients are allowed to cache the answer. No single number fits every case.

| Situation | Typical TTL | Why |
|-----------|-------------|-----|
| Stable production endpoint (e.g. API apex) | 300–3600 (5 min–1 h) | Balance cache hit rate and ability to change IPs with notice |
| Pre-migration or failover | 60–300 (1–5 min) | Short window so after you flip the record, most clients see it within minutes |
| CDN or load-balanced pool | Often 300–600 | Provider may override or suggest; you want some caching but not days |
| Static marketing site | 3600–86400 (1–24 h) | Rarely changes; long TTL reduces load on DNS and speeds lookups |
| Staging or ephemeral envs | 60–300 | You'll change IPs or tear down; keep TTL low so fixes stick quickly |

**Cutover drill:** Lower TTL to 60–300 at least one full TTL period *before* you change the record. Example: if current TTL is 3600, set it to 300, wait an hour (so old caches expire), then change the A/AAAA target. That way you avoid the "half the world still has the old IP" problem Raj hit.

---

## Runnable example 2: tracing resolution and checking authority

When "my domain doesn't resolve" or "I updated DNS but nothing changed", you want to see: (1) what your machine is actually getting, (2) what the authoritative server says, (3) whether there's a caching layer in between.

```bash
# 1. What your default resolver returns (often your ISP or corporate DNS)
dig +short docs.github.com A

# 2. Query the authoritative nameservers directly (bypass local cache)
# First get the NS for the zone
dig +short github.com NS
```

Example NS output:

```text
dns1.p08.nsone.net.
dns2.p08.nsone.net.
dns3.p08.nsone.net.
dns4.p08.nsone.net.
```

```bash
# 3. Ask one of those NS directly for the A record
dig @dns1.p08.nsone.net docs.github.com A +short
```

If the direct authority answer matches what you expect but your default resolver doesn't, the problem is caching (wait for TTL or flush local/recursive cache). If the authority answer is wrong, the bug is in your DNS config at the provider.

**Probe from elsewhere:** Your laptop might use a different resolver than production. Use a public resolver to simulate another view:

```bash
dig @8.8.8.8 docs.github.com A +short
dig @1.1.1.1 docs.github.com A +short
```

---

## Comparison: low TTL vs high TTL

| | Low TTL (e.g. 60–300 s) | High TTL (e.g. 3600–86400 s) |
|--|--------------------------|-------------------------------|
| **Pros** | Changes propagate quickly; fewer "stale IP" incidents after migrations | Fewer DNS queries, less load on auth servers, slightly faster repeat lookups from cache |
| **Cons** | More queries to your DNS provider; slightly more latency on cache miss | After a change, some users keep old IP until TTL expires |
| **When to use** | Before/after migrations, failover, or when the target IP changes often | Stable endpoints, static assets, when you rarely change the mapping |

We use 300 s for most production APIs and drop to 60 s the day before a planned cutover.

---

## Common pitfalls

1. **CNAME at the zone apex.** The apex is the domain itself (e.g. `example.com` with nothing in front). A CNAME at the apex can conflict with MX and other records and is not allowed by the standard. Use an A/AAAA record or a provider-specific "ALIAS" / "flattened" target that resolves to an IP on the provider's side.

2. **Forgetting to lower TTL before a change.** You change the A record; half the world still has the old IP for hours. Lower TTL first, wait at least one full old TTL, then switch.

3. **Assuming your change is live everywhere.** Browsers, OS, and recursive resolvers all cache. `dig` from your machine shows what *your* resolver returned; production might use a different resolver or a different region. Check from another network or use `dig @8.8.8.8` / `dig @1.1.1.1` to see another view.

4. **TXT record formatting.** TXT can have multiple strings; some providers show them concatenated, others as separate strings. For SPF/DKIM, a single string is usual; watch for accidental line breaks or extra quotes that break validation.

5. **CNAME and "other record" on the same label.** You cannot have both a CNAME and an A record for `www.example.com`. Pick one: either CNAME to another hostname or A/AAAA to IP(s).

---

## What went wrong (lessons learned)

On a migration in 2025, we moved an API from one cloud region to another. We updated the A record to the new load balancer IP and ran smoke tests from our office — all green. Within an hour, we got reports of timeouts from users in South America and Southeast Asia. Our office resolver had picked up the new IP quickly; resolvers in those regions were still serving the old one (TTL had been 7200). We had to lower TTL to 60, wait 2 hours, then change the record again. Downtime for those users was about 90 minutes. We now keep TTL at 300 for that record and have a runbook: "Before any IP or host change: set TTL to 60, wait 2× previous TTL, then apply change."

Another incident: Aiko added a CNAME for `api.example.com` pointing at a third-party API gateway. The provider required a TXT record on the same name for verification. The moment she added the TXT, DNS broke — their provider didn't allow CNAME + TXT on the same label (strict RFC behaviour). Fix was to use a subdomain like `gateway.api.example.com` for the CNAME and keep `api.example.com` as an A record or use the provider's "CNAME flattening" at the edge so the apex-like name wasn't a real CNAME in the zone. Lesson: check whether your DNS host allows CNAME plus other types; many do not.

---

## Actionable takeaway

1. **Audit TTLs** for any hostname that might change (APIs, LB targets). If they're above 600, document why; if you have a migration plan, include "lower TTL 1–2× current TTL before cutover".
2. **Run `dig` from your machine and from a public resolver** when debugging: `dig +short <name> A` and `dig @1.1.1.1 +short <name> A`. If they differ, it's cache or resolver-specific.
3. **Avoid CNAME at the zone apex.** Use A/AAAA or your provider's ALIAS/flattening for the root domain; use CNAME for subdomains (e.g. `www`, `api`) when you want to point at another hostname.
4. **Before adding a CNAME, check** whether that label already has (or will need) MX, TXT, or A. If it does, use a different subdomain or an A record.
5. **Keep a one-line runbook** for DNS changes: "TTL ≤ 300 for mutable targets; before cutover: set TTL to 60, wait 2× old TTL, then change record; verify with `dig @8.8.8.8 <name> A`."

Once you're used to reading `dig` output and thinking in TTLs, most DNS issues become quick to isolate — and you avoid the 3 AM "why is Asia still hitting the old server?" call.

---
